headline: Fake Go DNS scanner spread malware through over 200 GitHub repos
summary: A sophisticated malware campaign, 'Operation Muck and Load,' has published over 700 malicious modules since January, using a Go module disguised as a DNS scanner to infect Windows systems.
details: Supply-chain security firm Socket uncovered a Go module posing as a DNS and subdomain scanner, which actually functioned as a first-stage Windows malware loader. This module was traced to 222 GitHub repositories across 190 accounts.

The module, first published on January 24, has accumulated over 1,200 versions, with more than 700 of them being malicious. Socket, tracking the campaign as 'Operation Muck and Load,' reported it to the Go security team, leading to its block from the Go module proxy.

The extensive spread is attributed to the threat actor's GitHub Actions workflow, which generated a pseudo-version for each timed commit. This inflated a simple scanner utility's release history into hundreds of versions.

Across the confirmed repositories, a consistent workflow was observed: setting the Git email to ischhfd83@rambler.ru and force-pushing a rewritten log file every minute. This method created owner-attributed activity on disposable accounts while leaving a reusable fingerprint.

The module's `main.go` executes a hidden PowerShell command that downloads content from muckcoding.com. This content is then decoded with `certutil` and run with an execution-policy bypass, acting as a multi-layer loader using Base64 encoding and XOR decryption.

Instead of hardcoding payload URLs, the malware retrieves text from public platforms like Pastebin, YouTube, Instagram, and Telegram. It searches for a marker string, decrypts a trailing blob, and recovers the actual download location, allowing for dynamic updates.

The resolved URL leads to a password-protected 7-Zip archive hosted as a GitHub release asset. This archive is extracted into a directory mimicking a legitimate Microsoft Photos install, then launches `Microsoft.exe` with a hidden window.

Analysis revealed at least 14 unique malware files, including Trojan loaders, downloaders, Vidar infostealer, dropper, spyware payloads, and XMRig-related Monero cryptominers. These payloads map to various RATs like AsyncRAT, Quasar, and Remcos.

Lure themes for the malicious modules included MetaMask and Trust Wallet integrations, Binance and PayPal automation, Telegram and Discord bots, and game cheats for titles such as PUBG, Valorant, and Escape from Tarkov.

Socket assesses with high confidence that 'Operation Muck and Load' is linked to a cluster documented by Sophos in June last year. That research also identified the `ischhfd83@rambler.ru` address and the alias 'Muck,' which is embedded in domains like muckcoding.com.

headline: Flock cameras mistakenly track car reviewer over 'stolen' tags — police ambush tester in store parking lot and detain him for
summary: A car reviewer was ambushed by police and detained for an hour after Flock AI cameras misidentified his loaner Range Rover's license plate as stolen. A data entry error and the system's inability to read non-standard plates led to the incident.
details: A car reviewer for The Drive, Joel Feder, was driving a $155,000 loaner Range Rover when he was surrounded by four police cars in a parking lot. Officers informed him the vehicle's plate had been reported stolen and that they had been tracking him for days using the Flock app.

The hour-long detention revealed the issue stemmed from a data entry error in Flock's system. A different plate with similar characters (34 03 DTM) was reported stolen in California, but the LAPD report only listed '34 DTM', triggering a nationwide alert.

Compounding this, the Flock system misread Feder's New Jersey manufacturer plate (34 10 DTM). The system only registered the larger '34 DTM' and disregarded the smaller '10', flagging all vehicles with '34 ## DTM' as stolen.

Police had been tracking the vehicle for days but lost it when Feder parked in his covered garage. The retail store stop provided an opportunity for authorities to intercept him. Feder was advised to go straight home, as other agencies might still flag his car.

This incident adds to ongoing controversies surrounding Flock AI, including previous cases of police officers misusing the service to stalk individuals. Such events contribute to public distrust and pushback against surveillance technology.
